demographics: More common in females, roughly 4–5 times more often than males
Breech presentation is the strongest single risk factor
Left hip is affected more often than the right

risk_factors.text: Family history of developmental dysplasia of the hip
Swaddling with the hips and knees extended

comorbidities: Spina bifida or other neuromuscular conditions
family_history: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in a parent or sibling

chief_complaints.text: The doctor noticed one of her leg creases looks deeper than the other
Her legs don't seem to spread apart the same way when I change her diaper
She isn't walking yet, and she's almost 15 months old
She walks with a limp and waddles
The pediatrician heard a click in her hip at the check-up

hpi.onset: Present from birth; often detected at the newborn or well-child visit
hpi.duration: Detected in the first weeks to months of life, or later when the child begins to stand and walk
hpi.progression: The hip may be dislocatable at birth and either stabilize or progress to a fixed dislocation as the child grows and bears weight
hpi.location: One or both hips; the left hip is affected more often
hpi.quality: Painless in infancy; the parent notices asymmetry or difficulty spreading the legs rather than pain
hpi.severity: Mild in infancy; functional limitation becomes more apparent with walking

associated_symptoms.text: Unequal skin creases on the thighs or buttocks
The affected leg looks shorter than the other
The hip does not spread out as far as the other side
Clicking or clunking felt during hip examination

pertinent_negatives: Pain in the hip or leg
Refusal to bear weight after a fall
Swelling, redness or warmth over the hip
Weakness or loss of sensation in the legs
Loss of previously achieved motor milestones

positives.text: Unequal skin creases on the thighs or buttocks
The hip does not spread out as far as the other side
The affected leg looks shorter than the other

argues_against: Acute onset of hip pain with refusal to walk
Fever with a hot, swollen joint
Systemic illness with fever and irritability

atypical.how_it_differs: Newborns are usually completely asymptomatic; the only clue is a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver on screening examination, and the hips may be stable by the time of later visits.
Older infants and toddlers present with delayed walking, a limp or a waddling gait rather than a dislocatable hip; the dislocation is usually fixed and no longer reducible on examination.
Adults with untreated dysplasia present with hip pain, early osteoarthritis and a limp rather than the infantile screening findings.

general.moderate: Well-appearing but asymmetric leg position or limited hip motion noted on handling
general.severe: Older infant or toddler with a limp or waddling gait, otherwise well
general.critical: Not applicable; developmental dysplasia of the hip is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine and hips flexed to 90 degrees, abduct the hip while lifting the greater trochanter forward
findings.finding: A palpable clunk as the dislocated femoral head reduces into the acetabulum

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine and hips flexed, adduct the hip and apply posterior pressure along the femur
findings.finding: A palpable clunk as the femoral head dislocates posteriorly out of the acetabulum

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine, flex both hips and compare the degree of abduction on each side
findings.finding: The affected hip abducts less than the unaffected side

findings.maneuver: Inspect the thigh and buttock skin creases with the infant prone and supine
findings.finding: The skin creases on the affected thigh or buttock are deeper, more numerous or higher than on the other side

findings.maneuver: With the infant supine and hips and knees flexed with the feet flat on the table, compare knee heights
findings.finding: The knee on the affected side is lower than the other

findings.maneuver: Measure and compare the apparent length of both lower limbs
findings.finding: The affected leg appears shorter than the other

findings.maneuver: With the hip flexed, push and pull the femur along its long axis
findings.finding: Excessive piston-like movement of the femoral head along the shaft, indicating a fixed dislocation

findings.maneuver: Ask the child to stand on the affected leg and observe the pelvis
findings.finding: The pelvis drops on the unsupported side, indicating hip abductor weakness
A limp, or a waddling gait when both hips are affected

findings.maneuver: Ask about and palpate for hip or groin pain
findings.finding: No hip or groin pain in infancy; pain may be present in older children and adults with untreated dysplasia

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the hip region for swelling, warmth or erythema
findings.finding: No swelling, warmth or erythema over the hip

findings.maneuver: Assess lower limb tone, strength, sensation and deep tendon reflexes
findings.finding: Normal tone, strength, sensation and reflexes

imaging.preferred_when: Infants younger than 4-6 months, before the femoral head ossifies

findings.text: Femoral head sits outside the acetabulum or is only partially covered (dislocated or subluxated)
Shallow, steeply angled acetabular roof with a low alpha angle
Femoral head moves out of the socket with stress (dynamic instability)
Delayed or absent ossification of the femoral head ossific nucleus

imaging.preferred_when: Infants older than 4-6 months and older children, once the femoral head is ossified

findings.text: Femoral head displaced laterally and superiorly out of the acetabulum
Shallow, steep acetabular roof with a widened acetabular index (increased acetabular angle)
Delayed ossification of the femoral head ossific nucleus on the affected side
Disruption of Shenton's line (the smooth arc from the obturator foramen along the femoral neck is broken)
The ossific nucleus of the femoral head lies lateral to the vertical line drawn through the lateral edge of the acetabulum (positive Hilgenreiner line relationship)
Narrow teardrop figure and increased medial joint space

imaging.preferred_when: Older infants and children when the anteroposterior view is equivocal

findings.text: Confirms lateral and superior displacement of the femoral head
Better shows the shallow acetabulum and the relationship of the femoral head to the socket

imaging.preferred_when: Selected cases to assess the unossified femoral head, acetabular cartilage and soft tissue interposition before or after reduction

findings.text: Cartilaginous femoral head and acetabulum show the dysplastic relationship even before ossification
Ligamentum teres hypertrophy or pulvinar fat interposed in the socket

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely used; occasionally after reduction to assess the position of the femoral head within the acetabulum

findings.text: Femoral head position relative to the acetabulum after reduction

initial.why: First-line imaging in infants younger than 4-6 months; shows the cartilaginous femoral head and acetabulum and allows dynamic stress testing
initial.only_if: infant younger than 4-6 months with a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver, asymmetric skin creases, limited hip abduction or other risk factors

initial.why: First-line imaging once the femoral head ossifies, usually after 4-6 months of age
initial.only_if: infant older than 4-6 months or child with suspected dysplasia

supporting.why: Adds a second view when the anteroposterior film is equivocal
Assesses the unossified femoral head, acetabular cartilage and soft tissue interposition when plain imaging is not enough
supporting.only_if: surgical planning or concern for soft tissue interposition

not_indicated.why: No role; developmental dysplasia of the hip is not an infectious or inflammatory process
No role; there is no fever or systemic inflammation
No role; there is no fever or systemic inflammation
No role in an isolated hip dysplasia workup
Rarely needed and adds radiation; ultrasound and plain films are preferred

decision_points: Age determines the first imaging test: ultrasound before the femoral head ossifies (roughly younger than 4-6 months), plain x-ray after
Screen infants with a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver, asymmetric skin creases, limited hip abduction, breech presentation or a positive family history
Ultrasound is not useful after the femoral head ossifies; switch to plain radiographs
Refer to pediatric orthopedics when the diagnosis is confirmed or when the hip remains unstable

differential.name: Septic arthritis of the hip
differential.why_considered: An infant or child who will not move or bear weight on one leg can look like a dislocated hip
differential.trigger: Fever, irritability and refusal to move or bear weight on the affected leg

history: Acute onset over hours to days
Refusal to bear weight or move the leg
exam: Hip held in flexion, abduction and external rotation
Severe pain with any hip motion
labs: Blood cultures may grow an organism
Joint aspirate shows purulent fluid with organisms
imaging: X-ray may show widening of the joint space or later bony destruction

differential.name: Transient synovitis of the hip
differential.why_considered: A limping child with hip irritability is a common mimic of a hip problem

history: Mild pain, child still willing to bear weight
exam: Mild limitation of hip motion, especially internal rotation
labs: Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers
imaging: Ultrasound may show a small effusion
No dislocation or acetabular dysplasia on x-ray

differential.name: Proximal femoral focal deficiency
differential.why_considered: A short leg with an abnormal hip on examination and imaging can be mistaken for dysplasia

exam: Stable hip on Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers
imaging: X-ray shows a short or absent proximal femur with a normal acetabulum
The femoral head is not simply displaced out of a normal socket

differential.name: Coxa vara
differential.why_considered: A child with a limp and a short leg can have a decreased femoral neck-shaft angle rather than a dislocated hip

exam: Hip is stable on Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers
imaging: X-ray shows a reduced femoral neck-shaft angle with the femoral head still within the acetabulum
No lateral or superior displacement of the femoral head

differential.name: Cerebral palsy with hip subluxation
differential.why_considered: Neuromuscular imbalance can cause hip displacement and a waddling or scissoring gait

history: Abnormal tone or posture since infancy
Risk factors such as prematurity or perinatal asphyxia
imaging: Hip x-ray shows lateral displacement or subluxation with a dysplastic acetabulum
Brain MRI may show an underlying static encephalopathy

differential.name: Congenital muscular torticollis
differential.why_considered: It commonly coexists with developmental dysplasia of the hip and can be the first clue on examination

history: Head consistently tilted to one side
Often noted in the first weeks of life
exam: Palpable sternocleidomastoid tightness or a mass
Hip examination may be normal or abnormal
imaging: Neck ultrasound or x-ray confirms sternocleidomastoid fibrosis
Hip ultrasound is used to screen for coexisting dysplasia

differential.name: Metatarsus adductus
differential.why_considered: A foot deformity that is part of the same spectrum of intrauterine molding and is associated with developmental dysplasia of the hip

exam: Forefoot adducted with a convex lateral border
Hindfoot is flexible and corrects with gentle pressure
Hip examination may be normal or abnormal
imaging: Foot x-ray shows medial deviation of the metatarsals
Hip imaging is used to screen for coexisting dysplasia

severity.mild: Dislocatable or subluxatable hip with a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver, no fixed dislocation, and a normal acetabulum on imaging
severity.moderate: Persistent subluxation or early dislocation with a shallow acetabulum, asymmetric skin creases, limited hip abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign
severity.severe: Fixed dislocation with a markedly dysplastic acetabulum, leg length discrepancy, delayed walking and a limp or waddling gait
severity.critical: Not applicable; developmental dysplasia of the hip is not a life-threatening condition

red_flags.finding: Fever, irritability or refusal to bear weight
red_flags.meaning: Suggests septic arthritis or osteomyelitis rather than dysplasia; needs urgent aspiration and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Acute onset of hip pain after trauma
red_flags.meaning: Suggests fracture or slipped capital femoral epiphysis rather than a developmental problem

red_flags.finding: Progressive neurologic deficits or loss of milestones
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a neuromuscular or spinal cause of hip displacement

red_flags.finding: Bilateral fixed dislocations with a waddling gait
red_flags.meaning: Indicates severe, likely late-presenting disease that may need extensive surgical reconstruction

complications.name: Residual acetabular dysplasia
clues: Persistent shallow acetabulum on follow-up x-ray

complications.name: Early osteoarthritis of the hip
clues: Hip pain and stiffness in adolescence or young adulthood

complications.name: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
clues: Fragmentation or sclerosis of the ossific nucleus on x-ray
Persistent stiffness or pain after treatment

complications.name: Leg length discrepancy and gait abnormality
clues: Measured shortening of the affected limb

special_populations.differences: Newborns are usually asymptomatic; the only finding may be a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging before the femoral head ossifies.
Older infants and toddlers present with delayed walking, a limp or a waddling gait; the dislocation is often fixed and no longer reducible. Plain x-ray is the first-line imaging.
Adults with untreated dysplasia present with hip pain, early osteoarthritis and a limp rather than infantile screening findings; they may eventually need total hip arthroplasty.

key_questions.question: Was your baby born breech, or did you have low amniotic fluid during the pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Breech presentation or oligohydramnios, the strongest risk factors for developmental dysplasia of the hip

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of hip problems, hip dysplasia, or hip surgery in a parent or sibling?
key_questions.looking_for: A positive family history, which raises the risk and supports screening

key_questions.question: Have you noticed one of her thigh or buttock creases looking deeper or higher than the other?
key_questions.looking_for: Asymmetric skin creases, a classic clue to a dislocated or subluxated hip

key_questions.question: Do her legs spread apart the same way on both sides when you change her diaper?
key_questions.looking_for: Limited hip abduction on the affected side

key_questions.question: Did the doctor hear or feel a click or clunk in her hip at any visit?
key_questions.looking_for: A positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver noted on screening examination

key_questions.question: Has she started walking, and if so, does she limp or waddle?
key_questions.looking_for: Delayed walking or a limp or waddling gait in an older infant or toddler

key_questions.question: Does she seem to be in pain or cry when you move her legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent pain; pain and irritability suggest septic arthritis or another cause

key_questions.question: Has she had any fever, poor feeding, or been unwell recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; fever and systemic illness point away from dysplasia and toward infection

key_questions.question: Was she born first, and how much did she weigh at birth?
key_questions.looking_for: First-born and larger birth weight, both weakly associated with dysplasia

key_questions.question: How is she swaddled at home — are her legs wrapped straight and tight?
key_questions.looking_for: Tight swaddling with hips and knees extended, which can worsen hip position

key_questions.question: Has she had any trauma, fall, or refusal to bear weight on one leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; acute trauma or refusal to bear weight suggests fracture or slipped capital femoral epiphysis

key_questions.question: Has she lost any motor milestones she had previously reached, or does she have weakness in her legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; progressive weakness or milestone loss suggests a neuromuscular cause

reasoning_points: Infant with risk factors such as breech presentation, female sex, first-born status, or a positive family history
Asymmetric thigh or buttock skin creases and limited hip abduction on the affected side
Positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver indicating a dislocatable or reducible hip
Positive Galeazzi sign with the affected knee lower when hips and knees are flexed
Painless presentation without fever, swelling, or refusal to bear weight, which argues against infection
Hip ultrasound in an infant younger than 4–6 months, or anteroposterior pelvis x-ray once the femoral head has ossified
Imaging shows a shallow acetabulum with lateral or superior displacement of the femoral head
Older infants and toddlers may present with delayed walking, a limp, or a waddling gait rather than a dislocatable hip

easy: Newborn with a known breech presentation and a positive Ortolani or Barlow maneuver on the newborn examination
Infant with clearly asymmetric thigh creases and limited hip abduction on one side
Classic risk profile of a first-born female infant with a family history of hip dysplasia
Ultrasound confirms a dislocated hip with a shallow acetabulum
medium: Infant with only asymmetric skin creases and no palpable clunk, requiring ultrasound for confirmation
Older infant who is not yet walking and has a subtle leg length discrepancy
Bilateral dysplasia with a waddling gait and no obvious asymmetry between sides
Infant whose hips were stable at birth but who has limited abduction at the 4-month visit
hard: Toddler presenting with a limp and no history of hip clicking or abnormal newborn screening
Infant with coexisting congenital muscular torticollis or metatarsus adductus distracting from the hip
Child with a limp and mild hip pain where transient synovitis or septic arthritis must be excluded first
Adolescent or young adult with hip pain and early osteoarthritis from untreated dysplasia
Infant with normal skin creases and a normal Galeazzi sign but an abnormal ultrasound
